title: androiddump: Don't hang for 20s on Linux if loopback is down
description:
androiddump uses nonblocking connect on Windows, trying 10 times
with 1ms timeouts in select(). (This is short, but it's generally
trying to connect to the loopback interface.) On UN*X, it uses blocking
sockets, also trying 10 times, with SO_SNDTIMEO set to 2s.

Generally the socket returns nears instaneously, because it's
trying to connect to localhost. If the loopback interface goes
down, however, this results in 20s of timeouts.

Use non-blocking sockets on UN*X as well. Simplify some of the
handling; there's no real reason to set SO_SNDTIMEO (and then
change it again?) when in non-blocking mode, and there's no
good reason to have an extra sleep if there's a timeout in
the select.

Related to #13104, #15295

notes.body:
> On UN\*X, it uses blocking sockets

Is there a reason not to use non-blocking sockets on UN\*Xes?  [The POSIX page for `connect()`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/connect.html) says

> If the connection cannot be established immediately and O_NONBLOCK is set for the file descriptor for the socket, *connect*() shall fail and set errno to [EINPROGRESS], but the connection request shall not be aborted, and the connection shall be established asynchronously. Subsequent calls to *connect*() for the same socket, before the connection is established, shall fail and set *errno* to [EALREADY].
> 
> When the connection has been established asynchronously, [*pselect*()](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/pselect.html), [*select*()](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/select.html), and [*poll*()](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/poll.html) shall indicate that the file descriptor for the socket is ready for writing.

A good reason? No. That's what (AIUI) has to happen on non-Linux UN\*Xes anyway. This was just much quicker to write and have work properly on Linux without having to implement something with select or poll. My understanding is that the Windows implementation of select is slightly different; on UN*X you're supposed to retrieve `SO_ERROR` after the select returns because the select can indicate that the file descriptor is "ready for writing" after an error (Linux `select(2)` man page):

> After select(2) indicates writability,  use  getsockopt(2)  to  read  the SO_ERROR option at level SOL_SOCKET to determine whether connect() completed successfully (SO_ERROR is zero) or unsuccessfully (SO_ERROR  is  one  of  the usual  error  codes  listed  here, explaining the reason for the failure)

 but that doesn't seem to be done in the existing Windows code - I think because Windows always puts a FD with a failed connection into `exceptfds` instead of `writefds` to avoid having to do that.
OK, I did the proper handling for UN*X nonblocking.

> on UN\*X you're supposed to retrieve `SO_ERROR` after the select returns because the select can indicate that the file descriptor is "ready for writing" after an error

According to [the Single UNIX Specification page for`select()`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/select.html), that's the behavior for non-blocking `connect()`:

> If a descriptor refers to a socket, the implied output function is the [*sendmsg()*](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/sendmsg.html) function supplying an amount of normal data equal to the current value of the SO_SNDLOWAT option for the socket. If a non-blocking call to the [*connect()*](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/connect.html) function has been made for a socket, and the connection attempt has either succeeded or failed leaving a pending error, the socket shall be marked as writable.

and the SUS `getsockopt()` documentation, and pages to which it refers, specifies that `SO_ERROR` is one of the supported socket-level options.
